lead: The access matrix models every right a subject has on every object. It exists to give a clear, uniform view of protection. The model is used when an OS must decide whether a process can read a file, write a device, or execute a program. Real systems cannot store the full matrix, so they implement it as Access‑Control Lists (column‑wise) or capability lists (row‑wise).
prereq: You need: basic concepts of subjects and objects from Goals and principles of protection.

blocks.text: The matrix has subjects as rows and objects as columns. Each entry contains the set of rights the subject can exercise on the object. Rights are usually read (R), write (W), execute (X) or a combination. The matrix is also called a protection matrix in some courses.
If a cell is empty, the subject has no right on that object. The matrix gives a complete picture but can be very large in a real system.

blocks.where: M is the matrix; s is a subject row; o is an object column; rights is the set stored in that cell.

blocks.text: An ACL is stored with each object. It lists all subjects that have a right on that object and the specific rights. The OS checks the ACL of the target object when a request arrives.

items: Search the list for the requesting subject.
If the subject appears, verify that the required right is present.
Efficient for objects that have few subjects (short ACLs).
Revocation of a right means removing the subject from the ACL.

blocks.text: A capability list is stored with each subject. It contains a capability for every object the subject can access. A capability is a token that proves the holder’s rights.

items: The subject presents the required capability (a token) to the kernel, which checks the rights encoded in that token.
The kernel checks whether the capability for the target object includes the needed right.
Efficient for subjects that access few objects.
Transfer of a capability can be used for delegation.

figure.caption: The access matrix for three subjects and two objects. Notice the R entries for O1 and the W entries for O2.

spec.title: Access Matrix
spec.aria: Shows a 3×2 matrix where S1 can read object O1, S2 can write O2, and S3 can read O1 and write O2.

examples.question: Given the matrix in the figure, list the ACL for O1 and O2 and the capability list for subject S3. Then state the total number of granted rights in the matrix.
steps: Read column O1: entries are S1‑R and S3‑R. The ACL for O1 is {S1: R, S3: R}.
Read column O2: entries are S2‑W and S3‑W. The ACL for O2 is {S2: W, S3: W}.
Read row S3: entries are O1‑R and O2‑W. The capability list for S3 is {O1: R, O2: W}.
Count non‑empty cells: R at (S1,O1), R at (S3,O1), W at (S2,O2), W at (S3,O2). Total = 4 rights.
examples.answer: The ACLs are O1:{S1‑R, S3‑R} and O2:{S2‑W, S3‑W}. S3’s capability list is {O1‑R, O2‑W}. The matrix contains 4 granted rights.
examples.check:
rights = [['R','-'],['-','W'],['R','W']]
count = sum(1 for row in rights for cell in row if cell!='-')
print(count)

traps: Assuming the full matrix must be stored in RAM; real OSes use ACLs or capabilities to keep it sparse.
Confusing the direction: ACLs are attached to objects (columns), capabilities to subjects (rows).
Treating ‘-’ as a right instead of “no right”. This adds a false entry to the count.
Forgetting that revocation in an ACL means deleting the subject entry, not just clearing the right symbol.

quiz.q: What are the two dimensions of the access matrix?
quiz.a: Rows are subjects and columns are objects.

quiz.q: Why is the access matrix rarely stored completely in an operating system?
quiz.a: Because the matrix size grows with the product of subjects and objects, which can be very large; sparse storage via ACLs or capabilities saves memory.

quiz.q: Given a subject S that has a capability list {O1: R, O2: W}, can S read O2? State the answer and why.
quiz.a: No. The capability list shows S has only write (W) on O2. Read (R) is not granted.

quiz.q: If object O3 has an ACL {S1: X, S4: R}, what rights does S4 have on O3?
quiz.a: S4 has read (R) right on O3.

quiz.q: A system uses both ACLs and capabilities. A process presents a capability for O5 with rights {R,W}. The kernel also checks O5’s ACL and finds S2 with rights {R}. The process runs as S2. What effective rights does the process have on O5?
quiz.a: The process can only read (R). The capability grants {R,W} but the ACL for O5 grants only {R} to S2, so the effective rights are the intersection, i.e., read only.

quiz.q: What abbreviation is sometimes used for the access matrix?

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, capability ideas appear in microkernel designs and in hardware-enforced memory protection like CHERI. Research explores distributed capability systems where tokens are cryptographically signed. Cloud platforms use ACLs for storage buckets and API gateways. Next you may study attribute‑based access control (ABAC) which adds context to the matrix model.
